title: Concurrency: thread pools and async composition
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: ThreadPoolExecutor sizing, queue and maximumPoolSize behaviour, shutdown, Futures, CompletableFuture chains, virtual threads, concurrent.futures and asyncio gather/timeout.
source: Oracle Java docs (ThreadPoolExecutor, Executors, CompletableFuture, JEP 444 and JEP 491 on virtual threads, parallel streams); Python docs: asyncio, concurrent.futures, pickle; FastAPI docs; Java Concurrency in Practice; Baeldung; Real Python; Super Fast Python; Educative multithreading interview course

questions.prompt: new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 60, SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2)) receives 5 tasks that each block for a long time. How many worker threads exist after the 5 submissions?
questions.explanation: Tasks 1-2 start core threads. Tasks 3-4 fill the queue (capacity 2). Task 5 finds the queue full and the pool below maximumPoolSize, so a third thread is created. Threads beyond core are added only when the queue is full. Verified by running it.

questions.prompt: new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 10, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()) receives 100 tasks that each block for a long time. What is the largest number of worker threads that will ever exist?
questions.explanation: An unbounded queue never reports full, so the pool never grows past corePoolSize and maximumPoolSize is ignored. The 98 waiting tasks pile up in memory. This is the classic newFixedThreadPool pitfall.

questions.prompt: Using the sizing rule threads = cores x (1 + wait time / compute time), how many threads suit an 8-core machine whose tasks spend 90 ms waiting on a database and 10 ms computing?
questions.explanation: wait/compute = 90/10 = 9, so 8 x (1 + 9) = 80. For CPU-bound work use about cores (or cores + 1). Treat the formula as a starting point and load test.

questions.prompt: Match each Executors factory method with its main characteristic.

right.text: n core threads with an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue
Hands tasks over via SynchronousQueue and creates threads on demand without a limit
One worker thread, so tasks run strictly one after another
Runs tasks after a delay or repeatedly at a fixed rate
Starts a new virtual thread for every task (Java 21)

questions.explanation: Both fixed and cached pools have a trap: fixed has an unbounded queue (memory), cached has unbounded threads. Production code often builds a ThreadPoolExecutor by hand with a bounded queue.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentences about what happens when the queue is full and the pool is at maximumPoolSize.
questions.text: The default policy, {1}, throws RejectedExecutionException. {2} makes the submitting thread run the task itself, which slows producers down. {3} silently drops the new task.
questions.explanation: CallerRunsPolicy gives natural back-pressure. DiscardOldestPolicy drops the task at the head of the queue instead (ThreadPoolPolicy does not exist).

questions.prompt: Given ExecutorService pool, write the standard shutdown sequence: stop accepting tasks, wait up to 30 seconds for running tasks, and force-cancel if they did not finish.
questions.explanation: shutdown() lets queued work finish; shutdownNow() interrupts workers and returns the never-started tasks. Re-asserting the interrupt flag is good manners. Java 19+ also has ExecutorService.close() in try-with-resources.

questions.prompt: A task passed to ExecutorService.submit(...) throws a RuntimeException and nobody ever calls get() on the returned Future. What happens?

options.text: The exception is captured in the Future and silently lost.
options.why: Correct: submit wraps the task in a FutureTask that stores the failure until get() throws ExecutionException.

options.text: The exception is logged by the pool and the worker thread dies.
options.why: The default pool prints nothing for submit() tasks; with execute() the uncaught handler does run.

options.text: The whole ExecutorService shuts down immediately.
options.why: A task failure never shuts a pool down.

options.text: The exception is rethrown on the thread that called submit.
options.why: submit returns normally; the failure surfaces only through Future.get().

questions.explanation: With execute(Runnable) an uncaught exception reaches the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler. With submit() you must call get() or add logging inside the task.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

with ThreadPoolExecutor(3) as ex:
    print(list(ex.map(work, [3, 1, 2])))

where work(n) sleeps n tenths of a second and returns n.

options.text: [3, 1, 2], following the input order
options.why: Correct: map yields results in the order of the inputs, even though the 1 finishes first.

options.text: [1, 2, 3], following the finish order
options.why: That would be completion order, which is what as_completed gives, not map.

options.text: [3, 2, 1], sorted from largest to smallest
options.why: Nothing in map sorts results in descending order.

options.text: It prints in random order depending on the scheduler.
options.why: Result order from map is deterministic.

questions.explanation: Executor.map preserves input order (blocking on the earliest unfinished result); use as_completed(futures) to process in completion order. Exceptions are raised when the result is reached.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Executors.newFixedThreadPool is risky when tasks arrive faster than they complete.
questions.reason: Its LinkedBlockingQueue is unbounded, so the queue can grow until the JVM runs out of memory.

whys.a: Correct: the unbounded queue is the mechanism; the pool never rejects, it just queues.
whys.b: Both are true, but R is the direct reason, not an unrelated fact.
whys.c: R is true, so A is not the only true statement here.
whys.d: A is true: unbounded growth is a real production failure.

questions.explanation: Prefer a ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue and an explicit RejectedExecutionHandler.

questions.prompt: Assume CompletableFuture<User> fetchUser(int id) and CompletableFuture<List<Order>> fetchOrders(User u) already exist. Write one chained expression that fetches the user, then their orders, maps the result to the number of orders, and returns 0 if anything fails.

checks.label: chains the dependent call with thenCompose
handles failure with exceptionally or handle

questions.explanation: fetchOrders returns a future, so the step must be thenCompose (flatMap). exceptionally sees a CompletionException wrapping the real cause. Using handle((v, e) -> ...) is an equally valid answer.

questions.prompt: fetchOrders(user) returns CompletableFuture<List<Order>>. What type does userFuture.thenApply(u -> fetchOrders(u)) have?

options.text: CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<List<Order>>>
options.why: Correct: thenApply wraps whatever the function returns, giving a nested future.

options.text: CompletableFuture<List<Order>>, flattened by thenApply
options.why: That is what thenCompose returns by flattening the inner future.

options.text: List<Order>, unwrapped by blocking inside thenApply
options.why: thenApply never blocks to unwrap; you would call join() for that.

options.text: CompletableFuture<Void>, because the result is discarded
options.why: Only thenAccept/thenRun produce Void futures.

questions.explanation: thenApply is map, thenCompose is flatMap. allOf(...) returns CompletableFuture<Void>, so collect values by calling join() on the individual futures afterwards.

questions.prompt:
Consider the code below.

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("boom"); })
    .exceptionally(e -> { System.out.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName()); return 1; });

What class name does the handler print?

options.text: CompletionException
options.why: Correct: a failure from supplyAsync reaches downstream stages wrapped in a CompletionException; e.getCause() is the IllegalStateException.

options.text: IllegalStateException
options.why: The cause is unwrapped only via getCause(); the handler receives the wrapper here.

options.text: ExecutionException
options.why: ExecutionException is what Future.get() throws, not what stage callbacks receive.

options.text: RuntimeException
options.why: The wrapper is the more specific CompletionException subclass of it.

questions.explanation: Verified by running it. join() throws CompletionException, get() throws ExecutionException. Unwrap with getCause() when mapping errors.

questions.prompt: Write a Python coroutine fetch_all(urls) that calls the existing coroutine fetch(url) for every url concurrently and returns the list of results in input order, raising TimeoutError if the whole batch takes more than 2 seconds.

checks.label: runs the coroutines concurrently with gather
enforces a 2 second limit via wait_for or timeout

questions.explanation: gather returns results in argument order. On Python 3.11+ async with asyncio.timeout(2): return await asyncio.gather(...) is an equivalent alternative. On timeout the gathered awaitables are cancelled.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Awaiting three asyncio.sleep(1) coroutines with asyncio.gather finishes in about 1 second.
questions.reason: The asyncio event loop starts one thread per coroutine so that they run in parallel.

whys.a: A is true but R is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.b: R is false, so option b is wrong.
whys.c: Correct: the sleeps overlap because the single-threaded loop switches at each await. There is one thread, so R is false.
whys.d: A is true, so option d is wrong.

questions.explanation: asyncio is cooperative concurrency on one thread. A blocking call such as time.sleep(1) would serialise the three coroutines to about 3 seconds.

questions.prompt: A FastAPI endpoint declared with async def calls the blocking requests.get(...) and the service stalls under load. Select all valid fixes.

options.text: Declare the endpoint with plain def so FastAPI runs it in its thread pool
options.why: Correct: FastAPI runs sync endpoints in a worker thread, off the event loop.

options.text: Use an async HTTP client such as httpx.AsyncClient with await
options.why: Correct: it yields to the loop while waiting for the network.

options.text: Wrap the call in await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, url)
options.why: Correct: the blocking call runs in a thread while the loop stays free.

options.text: Add the async keyword to the helper that calls requests.get
options.why: Wrong: async def does not make blocking code non-blocking; it still stalls the loop.

options.text: Run the app with more asyncio tasks
options.why: Wrong: more tasks on a blocked loop just wait behind it.

questions.explanation: Rule: never block the event loop. Either stay async end to end, or push blocking work to a thread (to_thread, run_in_executor) or process pool.

questions.prompt: Java 21 virtual threads are the best fit for CPU-bound number crunching, because they are cheaper to create than platform threads.

options.text: True
options.why: Cheap creation helps blocking I/O concurrency, not CPU throughput.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: virtual threads are scheduled on a small pool of carrier threads, so CPU-bound work gains nothing over about one thread per core. They shine when many tasks mostly block on I/O.

questions.explanation: Virtual threads (JEP 444, final in Java 21) make thread-per-request affordable for blocking I/O, but they gain nothing for CPU-bound work, where parallelism is capped by cores. Do not pool them. On Java 21 a virtual thread blocking inside a synchronized block pins its carrier thread; JDK 24 (JEP 491) removed that pinning for synchronized, leaving mainly native frames and class initialisers.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

async def ok(): await asyncio.sleep(0.1); return 1
async def bad(): raise ValueError("x")
async def main():
    print(await asyncio.gather(ok(), bad(), return_exceptions=True))
asyncio.run(main())

options.text: [1, ValueError('x')]
options.why: Correct: with return_exceptions=True failures are returned in the result list in argument order, and the other awaitables still finish.

options.text: ValueError: x is raised and nothing is printed
options.why: Wrong: that is the default behaviour (return_exceptions=False); here the exception is delivered as a value.
Wrong: results are never dropped; the failed slot holds the exception object.

options.text: [ValueError('x'), 1]
options.why: Wrong: gather keeps results in the order of its arguments, not in completion order.

questions.explanation: With the default False the first exception propagates to the awaiter while the other awaitables keep running; on Python 3.11+ asyncio.TaskGroup cancels the siblings instead. Verified by running it.

questions.prompt: A Java service calls list.parallelStream().forEach(item -> blockingHttpCall(item)). Which problem is most likely?

options.text: Blocking calls tie up the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool, starving other parallel work
options.why: Correct: parallel streams share one small common pool sized near the core count, so blocking tasks hold its few workers.

options.text: Every element gets its own new virtual thread, which eventually exhausts the available memory
options.why: Wrong: parallel streams use ForkJoinPool workers (platform threads), not virtual threads.

options.text: forEach on a parallel stream always runs on the calling thread, so nothing is parallel
options.why: Wrong: work is split across the common pool workers plus the caller, which is the source of the sharing problem.

options.text: The stream silently falls back to sequential execution whenever it sees blocking I/O calls
options.why: Wrong: the stream has no idea about blocking; it keeps splitting tasks regardless.

questions.explanation: Parallel streams suit CPU-bound, side-effect-free work on big in-memory collections. For blocking I/O use an executor sized for I/O or virtual threads.

questions.prompt: On JDK 24 or later (JEP 491), select all situations that can still pin a virtual thread to its carrier thread.

options.text: A native or foreign-function frame is on the stack while the code blocks
options.why: Correct: a virtual thread cannot unmount while a native frame sits between it and the carrier.

options.text: The code is running inside a class static initializer when it blocks
options.why: Correct: class initialisation is one of the remaining pinning cases.

options.text: Blocking I/O inside a synchronized block
options.why: Wrong: JEP 491 lets a virtual thread unmount inside synchronized, which was the main pinning source in Java 21.

options.text: Calling Object.wait() while holding the monitor
options.why: Wrong: JDK 24 lets the virtual thread release its carrier while waiting, then reacquire the monitor.

options.text: Waiting on a contended ReentrantLock
options.why: Wrong: java.util.concurrent locks park the virtual thread and never pinned it, in any release.

questions.explanation: On Java 21 the synchronized cases did pin, which is why advice then was to use ReentrantLock around blocking calls. Check with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads on 21 or the jdk.VirtualThreadPinned JFR event.

questions.prompt: Why does executor.submit(lambda x: x * x, 3) fail with a PicklingError on a ProcessPoolExecutor, while a module-level def sq(x) works?

options.text: The callable and its arguments are pickled to reach another process, and a lambda cannot be pickled by reference
options.why: Correct: pickle stores functions by qualified name, which a lambda does not have. Verified by running it.

options.text: Lambdas are not allowed to return values across threads
options.why: Wrong: lambdas return values normally; the limit comes from serialisation to a separate process, not from return values.

options.text: The GIL forbids anonymous functions in worker threads
options.why: Wrong: ProcessPoolExecutor uses processes, and the GIL has no rule about function syntax.

options.text: ProcessPoolExecutor only accepts built-in functions
options.why: Wrong: any picklable top-level function works, as the sq example shows.

questions.explanation: Same rule for arguments and results: they must be picklable. ThreadPoolExecutor has no such limit because it shares memory.
